claims.text: As-received, untreated Q235 steel has a native, non-optimized iron oxide film on its surface.
The integrity of the native iron oxide film governs the onset or suppression of corrosion in Q235 steel.
Chloride-containing environments degrade the native oxide film on Q235 steel.
Elevated temperature accelerates degradation of the native oxide film through chemical attack and thermal stress.
Native-film breakdown occurs preferentially at grain boundaries and inclusion sites.
Discontinuities in the oxide film create localized anodic sites.
Localized anodic sites promote pitting and accelerated corrosion.
A denser, more adherent, intentionally stabilized oxide film retains barrier properties and suppresses corrosion initiation.
Controlled pre-oxidation can modify the thickness, porosity, adhesion, and stability of the Q235 surface oxide.
Mechanical polishing removes the native oxide film from Q235 steel.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution is an applicable environment for corrosion testing of Q235-based specimens.
Pre-oxidized Q235 specimens will have lower mass loss than untreated specimens.
Pre-oxidized Q235 specimens will have lower pit density than untreated specimens.
Polished specimens lacking the native oxide will exhibit earlier and faster corrosion than untreated specimens.
The predicted differences among pre-oxidized, untreated, and polished specimens will occur at both room temperature and approximately 70°C.
The predicted treatment effects will be more pronounced at approximately 70°C than at room temperature.
The proposed mechanism may depend on exposure duration, exact temperature, grain-boundary density, inclusion distribution, and intrinsic material variability.
The proposed mechanism is limited to Q235 steel in chloride-rich aqueous environments and may not transfer to other steels or aggressive species.
